title: The Present Perfect Tense
keyIdea: The present perfect is has or have plus the past participle: she has eaten, they have gone. Use has with he, she, it or one name, and have with I, you, we and they. It links the past to now: I have lost my key means the key is still lost. The simple past tells about a finished time: I lost my key last week. So finished-time words like yesterday, last week and ago go with the simple past, while already, yet, ever, never and since go with has or have. Has gone means still away; has been means there and back.
familyTip: Play 'Have you ever?' at dinner. Take turns asking: Have you ever seen a fox? Answer with Yes, I have seen one, or No, I have never seen one. If someone adds a when, like last summer, switch to the simple past together: I saw one last summer. Listen out for has gone and has been when someone leaves the house and comes back.

visual.caption: Finished time or up to now? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: I have fed the cat, so it is happy.
We went to the zoo last May.
We have never been to a zoo.
He broke his arm two weeks ago.
He has broken his arm, so he can’t swim.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build has/have + participle, match sentences to timelines, sort time words, place Dad for gone or been, fix the slip.

kid: Some verbs have two parts. First has or have. Then a verb like eaten, gone or seen. She has eaten. They have gone. This is the present perfect.
Use has for one person or thing: he has, she has, Tom has. Use have for I, you, we and they. After has or have, say eaten, not ate. Say gone, not went.
I ate lunch at 12. That time is over. I have eaten, so I am not hungry. That one links to now. Words like yesterday and last week go with ate. Words like already, yet and ever go with have eaten.
Dad has gone to the park. He is still there. Dad has been to the park. He went and came back.
adult: Ages 7 to 11. The National Curriculum in England introduces the present perfect in Year 3 (English Appendix 2: the present perfect form of verbs in contrast to the past tense, e.g. He has gone out to play contrasted with He went out to play) and uses it in Upper KS2 writing. CCSS L.5.1b asks for perfect verb tenses. Key words: present perfect, simple past, auxiliary verb (has, have), past participle, irregular verb, time adverbial.

Form: has or have, chosen to agree with the subject, plus the past participle. For regular verbs the past participle looks the same as the simple past (finished, played), which hides the difference; irregular verbs show it (ate and eaten, went and gone, saw and seen, wrote and written). Use: the present perfect links a past event to the present (a result now, an experience up to now, or something still continuing with since or for), while the simple past places the event at a finished time.

Common mistakes: using the simple past form after has or have (I have went, she has ate); she have instead of she has; putting a finished-time word with the present perfect (I have seen it yesterday), which is ungrammatical in standard British and American English; Has you instead of Have you; and confusing has gone (still away) with has been (went and came back). American English sometimes uses the simple past with already and yet (Did you eat yet?), so children may hear both.

In the lab your child builds sentences from has or have plus a participle, drags sentences onto a finished-time or linked-to-now timeline, sorts time words, decides where Dad or Mia is now after has gone and has been, and finds the one wrong word in a line. Each wrong choice gets a reason.

practice.hint: They takes have. Then use the past participle of finish.
practice.explain: They have finished: have agrees with they, and finished is the past participle.

practice.prompt: Each present perfect verb has 2 words, like has eaten. A story has {n} present perfect verbs. How many words do those verbs use?
practice.hint: Count 2 words for each one: has or have, plus the participle.
practice.explain: {n} verbs with 2 words each is {=2*n} words.

practice.prompt: Which time word fits? I have ___ seen that film.
practice.hint: Yesterday and last week are finished times. Which word links to now?
practice.explain: I have already seen that film. Yesterday and last week need the simple past: I saw that film yesterday.

practice.prompt: Mia has gone to the shop. She left {n} minutes ago. Where is Mia now?
choices: At the shop or on the way
practice.hint: Has gone means she went and is not back yet.
practice.explain: Has gone: Mia is still away. If she had come back, we would say Mia has been to the shop.

practice.prompt: Which one means the key is still lost now?
choices: I lost my key on Monday.
practice.hint: Which one links the past to now?
practice.explain: I have lost my key tells you it is still lost. I lost my key on Monday is about a finished time; I may have found it since.

pool.hint: Look for has or have plus a past participle.
pool.explain: Has written is has plus the past participle written. Wrote is simple past and is writing is the progressive.

pool.prompt: Gran came to tea yesterday. Which sentence about it is right?
pool.explain: A finished time like yesterday takes the simple past: I saw Gran yesterday.

pool.prompt: Ben has been to the park. He was there for {n} minutes. Where is Ben now?
choices: On his way to the park
pool.hint: Has been means there and back.
pool.explain: Has been: Ben went to the park and came back. Has gone would mean he is still there.

pool.prompt: We moved here {n} years ago and we still live here. We have lived here for how many years?
pool.hint: Have lived runs from the move right up to now.
pool.explain: We have lived here for {n} years: the present perfect covers the time from the move up to now.

pool.prompt: Which word fits? He ___ broken his arm.
pool.hint: He is one person, and one person takes has: he has, she has, it has.
pool.explain: He has broken his arm. Has goes with he, she, it and one name.

pool.prompt: Which word fits? We have ___ to the beach.
pool.hint: After have, use the past participle.
pool.explain: We have gone to the beach. Went is the simple past and cannot follow have.

pool.prompt: Which time word goes with the present perfect?
pool.hint: Which one is not a finished time?
pool.explain: I have never been to Spain. Two days ago and in 2019 are finished times, so they take the simple past.

pool.hint: You takes have, and the verb needs its past participle.
pool.explain: Have you finished yet? Have agrees with you, and finished is the past participle.

pool.prompt: Why does the writer say He has gone out instead of He went out?
choices: He went out a long time ago
pool.hint: The present perfect links the past to now.
pool.explain: He has gone out tells you he is still out. He went out just tells you something that happened at a past time.
